question: In a solvable high-dimensional sequence-to-token task, how do initially redundant softmax-attention heads specialize under SGD, and can a different across-head normalization suppress redundant-head noise and attain Bayes risk?

key_findings.claim: Author model: a planted single-location regression task turns head specialization into symmetry breaking among a finite committee of attention keys.
key_findings.evidence: Each sequence has one uniformly hidden relevant token whose mean is a random combination of F shared Gaussian spikes; H learned key vectors attend to the tokens and their outputs are uniformly averaged. In the D to infinity limit, alignments m, head overlaps q, and orthogonal amplitude r suffice to express the population loss.

anchors.section: Appendix A.1 proof of Proposition III.1

key_findings.claim: Author theorem: under a high-dimensional small-step scaling, online SGD order parameters converge to a closed gradient-flow system.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition III.2 evolves m, r, biases, and the output scale by gradients of the reparameterized population loss. The proof invokes localizability and an external high-dimensional SGD limit; the stated regime requires gamma/Nb=o(D^-1), covering Nb proportional to D with vanishing gamma or fixed Nb with gamma=o(D^-1), rather than ordinary finite-learning-rate SGD.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2.a sample complexity of SGD
Lemma A.3 high-dimensional limit of SGD

key_findings.claim: Author theorem: when the latent-feature mean is nonzero, every head first moves together along that mean in O(1) effective time before specialization.
key_findings.evidence: Permutation symmetry makes the unspecialized manifold invariant, while the gradient at zero points along E[theta]. Proposition III.3 therefore gives a common O(1) alignment after a finite time; the appendix translates this to a total sample requirement omega(D) under its learning-rate scaling.

key_findings.claim: Author theorem: small random asymmetries escape the unspecialized saddle after logarithmic effective time and produce O(1) head differences along nondegenerate covariance directions.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition III.4 assumes a nondegenerate covariance component orthogonal to the mean and sufficiently small mean signal and initialization. Its SDE argument amplifies diffusive perturbations along negative-Hessian directions, yielding a stated specialization time Theta(log D); the appendix's quantitative sample argument is O(D^(1+2 zeta) log D) for arbitrarily small positive zeta.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2.b escaping the invariant subspace

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the appendix does not establish the high-probability sample-complexity claim printed in Lemma A.5.
key_findings.evidence: The lemma heading says the O(D^(1+2 zeta) log D) escape occurs with high probability, but its Paley-Zygmund calculation concludes only a probability Theta(1). No repetition, concentration, or bootstrapping step upgrades constant success probability to high probability; the main text's cleaner Theta(D log D) phrasing also suppresses the D^(2 zeta) slack.

key_findings.claim: Author result with mixed evidence levels: latent covariance eigenvectors are acquired from largest to smallest, but only the initial instability is analytic and the later saddle-to-saddle path is heuristic/numerical.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma III.1 identifies the earliest descent directions through a quadratic expansion. Result III.1 then extends this to sequential specialization and claims that softmax/softmax-1 heads learn signed mixtures of features, whereas Bayes-softmax heads tend toward individual directions; the paper explicitly says the later-time part relies on landscape heuristics and numerical integration.

key_findings.claim: Author conjecture, not theorem: rescaled specialization time should concentrate to a sharp dynamical phase transition.
key_findings.evidence: Conjecture III.1 proposes convergence of tau_s/log(sqrt(D)/eta) to a deterministic value. Appendix B linearizes escape around the unspecialized saddle and obtains the prediction heuristically; 100-run simulations show shrinking variation as initialization decreases, but at fixed D residual data-dependent variation remains.

key_findings.claim: Author theorem: Bayes-softmax exactly implements the posterior-mean predictor when the latent mixing distribution has finite support and one head is assigned per support point.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition IV.1 derives the posterior probability of the relevant token; Proposition IV.2 rewrites the resulting mixture-of-exponentials normalization as a joint normalization across heads and tokens. This is a representational existence result assuming access to the learned spike combinations and distribution weights, not a general optimization theorem.

anchors.section: Appendix A.3 proof of Proposition IV.1

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the prescription that the optimal head count equals the support size is task-specific and the claim that SGD reaches the Bayes solution is numerical.
key_findings.evidence: The exact correspondence uses a discrete known latent mixture and joint head-token normalization. Continuous mixtures require approximation as H grows. Figure 4 reports five numerical runs and is described once as a 'numerical guarantee,' but no theorem proves gradient flow reaches the global Bayes-softmax minimum from random initialization.

key_findings.claim: Author theorem: ordinary softmax and input-independent value weighting cannot eliminate error for signal distributions containing opposite regions, while softmax-1 can approach zero error at large signal.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition IV.3 attributes the gap to heads that must always distribute unit mass across tokens; softmax-1 can use its extra sink term to deactivate a badly aligned head. The large-signal construction is explicit in Appendix A.3.

anchors.section: Appendix A.3 proof of Proposition IV.3

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the printed impossibility proof for softmax-v silently needs a sign restriction that the model does not impose.
key_findings.evidence: Softmax-v permits learned real coefficients v_h. The proof obtains sum_h v_h approximately 1 and then lower-bounds a weighted sum of positive, head-dependent terms using that identity. This conclusion is invalid when some v_h are negative; neither the model definition nor Proposition IV.3 constrains v_h to be nonnegative, so the stated proof does not establish the softmax-v case as written.

key_findings.claim: Author numerics: finite-D SGD tracks the order-parameter ODE closely in the examined synthetic settings, and deactivating normalizations outperform softmax when signals change sign.
key_findings.evidence: At D=10,000 the reported SGD points visually follow the predicted curves for flipping-spike and anisotropic-Gaussian tasks. Five-run terminal-loss comparisons show the Bayes-softmax closest to Bayes risk and softmax-1 improving over standard softmax most clearly for isotropic sign-varying signals.

key_findings.claim: Author semi-realistic check: on an MNIST-patch detection task, Bayes-softmax heads look more digit-specific and deactivating activations slightly reduce error.
key_findings.evidence: Sequences contain one centered MNIST digit patch and four Gaussian-noise patches at fixed D=784 and signal 0.3. Figure 5 shows learned head images and a narrow error range; Appendix C supplies the data construction but no uncertainty intervals or standard transformer baseline.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the pruning result shows redundancy only inside the constructed task and does not validate a mechanism for redundancy in trained language models.
key_findings.evidence: Greedy pruning over five runs suggests roughly H-F heads can be removed before large loss increases. The task has a known F-dimensional latent signal, identity values, uniform aggregation, and no residual or output path, so one-head-per-feature behavior is largely built into the experiment's effective rank.

method.core_idea: Reduce high-dimensional online SGD for a planted multi-index, single-location attention task to a finite order-parameter flow, then analyze symmetry breaking and compare normalizations that can or cannot deactivate redundant heads.
method.mechanism: Head-spike alignments m capture signal learning, r captures components orthogonal to the planted subspace, and permutation symmetry defines an invariant unspecialized manifold. A nonzero mean signal drives a common fast alignment; initialization/SGD fluctuations are exponentially amplified along negative-Hessian covariance eigenmodes, producing slower specialization. A joint normalization across heads and tokens is matched to the Bayesian posterior, while a softmax-1 sink allows head deactivation.
assumptions: Embedding dimension tends to infinity while sequence length L, feature count F, head count H, signal strengths, and initialization scale stay fixed.
Every training step receives a fresh independent batch from the planted Gaussian sequence model.
The learning-rate/batch scaling gamma/Nb=o(D^-1) is used to obtain deterministic population gradient flow.
The attention-only predictor uses identity values, no output projection, no residual/MLP path, and uniform aggregation across heads.
Shared spike vectors are asymptotically orthogonal Gaussian directions and nuisance tokens are isotropic Gaussian noise.
The specialization proposition additionally needs sufficiently small mean signal and initialization and a nondegenerate covariance component orthogonal to the mean.
The sequential ordering beyond the initial Hessian instability is inferred heuristically and numerically.
Exact Bayes-softmax optimality for finite H assumes a discrete latent-mixture support represented by the heads with correctly set biases.
The softmax-1 well-specification result takes a large-signal limit after D tends to infinity.
Numerical order-parameter integration approximates population expectations by a fixed Monte Carlo sample reused across optimization steps.

techniques.role: Expresses risk and training using head-feature alignments, overlaps, and orthogonal amplitudes.
Maps fresh-batch SGD under a small-step scaling to a finite gradient flow and a rescaled SDE near saddles.
Separates a common unspecialized manifold from head-difference directions.
Orders initial symmetry-breaking modes by latent covariance eigenvalues.
Rewrites the Bayes posterior over token location as joint head-token softmax normalization.
Compares standard softmax, learned value weights, softmax-1 sinks, and Bayes-softmax.
Compares theoretical flows with synthetic SGD trajectories at D=10,000.
Provides a fixed-dimensional semi-realistic check using one digit among Gaussian-noise patches.

evaluations.setting: Flipping-spike and anisotropic-Gaussian synthetic tasks at D=10,000
evaluations.metric: Population loss, feature alignments, head differences, and orthogonal norm over effective time
evaluations.result: Finite-D SGD dots visually track the closed order-parameter trajectories for softmax, softmax-1, and Bayes-softmax in the reported configurations.
evaluations.baseline: Direct comparison to the asymptotic ODE; no finite-D error bars or convergence-rate fit.

evaluations.setting: Activation/normalization comparison over head count and signal strength
evaluations.result: Across five runs, Bayes-softmax is closest to Bayes risk; softmax-1 gains most over softmax for sign-varying isotropic signals, while learned static value weights do not close the gap.
evaluations.baseline: Standard softmax, softmax-v, softmax-1, and analytic Bayes risk.

evaluations.metric: Mean and standard deviation of rescaled specialization time over 100 runs
evaluations.result: Variation decreases with smaller initialization and larger D, supporting but not proving the phase-transition conjecture; fixed-D MNIST directions retain feature-dependent times.
evaluations.baseline: Heuristic exponential-escape prediction from Appendix B.

evaluations.metric: Final prediction error and visualized learned key vectors
evaluations.result: Bayes-softmax produces more visibly digit-specific heads and deactivating activations attain slightly lower reported error than standard softmax.
evaluations.baseline: The four normalization variants; no conventional cross-attention or classifier baseline.

evaluations.setting: Greedy pruning of H=8 trained heads
evaluations.result: Roughly H-F heads can often be removed with small degradation; deactivating variants degrade more sharply after necessary heads are removed.
evaluations.baseline: Standard softmax versus softmax-1 and Bayes-softmax over five runs.

limitations: Author-stated: the model has one attention layer, no output projection or residual path, and a stylized sequence-to-token regression distribution.
Author-stated: extension to deeper architectures and structured data remains open.
Reviewer-identified: the deterministic flow uses a very small learning-rate regime with fresh independent batches, not typical transformer training.
Reviewer-identified: head count, feature count, and sequence length stay fixed as dimension grows.
Reviewer-identified: Proposition III.4 needs small mean signal and initialization; its broader validity is only numerical.
Reviewer-identified: Result III.1 is only locally analytic, with later sequential specialization based on heuristic landscape arguments.
Reviewer-identified: the sharp phase transition is explicitly conjectural.
Reviewer-identified: Lemma A.5 proves only constant-probability escape despite claiming high probability.
Reviewer-identified: the softmax-v impossibility proof lacks a nonnegativity assumption on learned value weights.
Reviewer-identified: exact Bayes-softmax expressivity does not prove random-initialized SGD reaches the Bayes parameters.
Reviewer-identified: MNIST detection is a single relevant patch among isotropic noise, not language modeling or natural cross-attention.
Reviewer-identified: most terminal-loss and pruning plots use five runs, and several figures omit uncertainty intervals.
failure_modes: Finite learning rates or correlated minibatches produce SGD noise/drift outside the derived flow scaling.
Residual, value, output, or MLP pathways absorb redundant-head noise, reversing the normalization ranking.
Feature means or covariances are degenerate, eliminating the proposed fast/slow separation or ordering.
Latent directions are not low-rank Gaussian spikes and do not admit a fixed finite order-parameter closure.
A continuous or multimodal latent distribution needs far more heads than its low-dimensional examples suggest.
Random initialization selects an unbalanced late-time head configuration or the flow becomes trapped away from the Bayes-softmax solution.
Learned signed value weights cancel redundant outputs, invalidating the claimed softmax-v lower bound.
Empirical specialization in a deep transformer reflects task routing, layer interactions, or optimizer effects absent from the committee model.
A fixed Monte Carlo quadrature creates smoother optimization trajectories than fresh population estimates.
Apparent head specialization is basis-dependent: rotations within equal-covariance eigenspaces change individual alignments without changing function.
reusable_insights: Separate common-mode head learning from head-difference modes before interpreting specialization.
Track both signal-subspace alignments and orthogonal head components; low loss alone hides redundancy.
Treat Hessian ordering as a local prediction and test whether later feature acquisition actually follows it.
Distinguish representational Bayes optimality from optimizer convergence to the Bayes parameters.
Across-head normalization can implement mixture posterior weights that per-head normalization cannot.
Evaluate learned value/output paths before concluding that inactive attention heads necessarily inject irreducible variance.
When claiming high-probability saddle escape, supply concentration beyond a constant-probability second-moment argument.
Compare phase-transition times after explicitly controlling initialization scale and embedding dimension.
Use rank-controlled natural tasks to test whether one-head-per-latent-component behavior survives outside planted data.
open_questions: Can the order-parameter closure be extended to learned value matrices, output projections, residuals, and multiple layers?
Does ordinary finite-step SGD retain the same specialization ordering outside gamma/Nb=o(D^-1)?
Can the specialization-time conjecture be proved with a limiting distribution and finite-D error bounds?
What additional argument upgrades Lemma A.5 from constant to high probability?
Is Proposition IV.3 true for unrestricted signed softmax-v coefficients, or can static cancellations defeat the claimed lower bound?
Under what initialization conditions does Bayes-softmax gradient flow converge globally to the posterior representation?
How many heads are needed to approximate a continuous P_theta at a specified excess risk?
Do head-specific gates, softmax-1, and joint Bayes-softmax retain their ranking in trained language models?
How identifiable are specialized heads within degenerate latent eigenspaces?
Can real training checkpoints exhibit the predicted D log D separation after controlling optimizer and data order?

competitive_landscape.title: Attention layers provably solve single-location regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Marion et al. introduce single-location regression and prove asymptotic Bayes optimality/training properties for a simplified nonlinear attention predictor. The present paper adds multiple planted features and heads to study symmetry breaking and normalization, but remains within the same stylized task family.

competitive_landscape.title: Statistical Advantage of Softmax Attention: Insights from Single-Location Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Duranthon et al. characterize population and finite-sample generalization and contrast softmax with linear activations. This paper instead emphasizes multi-head training trajectories and proposes joint Bayes-softmax normalization, with less finite-sample risk analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Asymptotics of SGD in Sequence-Single Index Models and Single-Layer Attention Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Arnaboldi et al. derive closed high-dimensional SGD dynamics for semantic and positional alignments in sequence single-index models. The present work extends the flavor to multiple latent features and heads and focuses on head symmetry breaking.

competitive_landscape.title: Fundamental limits of learning in sequence multi-index models and deep attention networks: High-dimensional asymptotics and sharp thresholds
competitive_landscape.difference: Troiani et al. derive Bayes and algorithmic thresholds for sequence multi-index models and tied low-rank deep attention, including sequential layer learning. This paper studies online optimization of a shallower multi-head predictor rather than information/computation thresholds.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Dynamics of Multi-Head Softmax Attention for In-Context Learning: Emergence, Convergence, and Optimality
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. prove warm-up, task allocation, convergence, and near-optimality for multi-task in-context linear regression. Their heads allocate to tasks; here heads learn mixtures of planted feature directions and global convergence is not established.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Dynamics of In-Context Learning in Linear Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. derive principal-component acquisition and saddle-to-saddle dynamics for multi-head linear self-attention, with outcomes depending on merged versus separate Q/K parameterization. This paper finds covariance-ordered specialization in nonlinear softmax attention on a different planted retrieval task.

competitive_landscape.title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. track functional differentiation and multigram circuits in a trained two-layer attention-only transformer using refined learning coefficients. The present paper supplies a planted-model mechanism but does not test whether its covariance ordering explains those empirical circuits.

competitive_landscape.title: Loss Landscape Degeneracy and Stagewise Development in Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Hoogland et al. empirically associate developmental stages with loss-landscape degeneracy in language and ICL transformers. This paper derives a specific Hessian-driven symmetry-breaking story in a solvable regression model, without an LLC comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: From Attention to Activation: Unravelling the Enigmas of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Kaul et al. introduce softmax-1 empirically to mitigate attention sinks and activation outliers in language models. The present paper repurposes its sink as a head-deactivation mechanism and proves a large-signal existence result only in the planted task.

competitive_landscape.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
competitive_landscape.difference: Qiu et al. show query-dependent per-head sigmoid gates improve large language models and suppress sinks. Their learned gate is a practical deactivation route absent from the paper's parameter-free Bayes-softmax comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Multi-Head Attention as Ensemble Nadaraya-Watson Estimation: Variance Reduction, Decorrelation, and Optimal Head Diversity
competitive_landscape.difference: Fokoue analyzes head diversity through kernel-estimator covariance and principal angles under a fixed dimension budget. It offers a variance-reduction account of specialization distinct from this paper's SGD symmetry-breaking and redundant-output variance mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Flow Structure and Quantitative Dynamics of Multi-Head Self-Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: Pendharkar studies token clustering under fixed multi-head self-attention flows and identifies geometric interference between heads. The target paper instead learns the head parameters by SGD and studies feature alignment rather than token-state clustering.

competitive_landscape.title: A Mean-Field Analysis of Multi-Head Self-Attention under Cross-Entropy Training
competitive_landscape.difference: Huan and Yuan take an infinite-head measure-valued limit for causal self-attention under cross-entropy and state explicit extra conditions for convergence/stability. This paper instead takes embedding dimension large at fixed H under squared loss and derives finite order parameters.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first exact high-dimensional SGD account in this single-location multi-head setting, a two-stage hierarchy of head specialization, and a Bayes-softmax normalization that both prescribes head count and reaches Bayes risk.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper derives an order-parameter loss and small-step SGD limit, proves local unspecialized/specialization statements under restrictive assumptions, derives a posterior-equivalent joint normalization, and supports later-time behavior with synthetic and MNIST-patch numerics.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The cleanest novelty is the combination of multi-head symmetry breaking with single-location/multi-index order parameters and the posterior interpretation of joint head-token normalization. Sequential late-time specialization and a sharp transition are not fully proved; global optimizer convergence is numerical; and two appendix claims have identifiable proof gaps. Novelty is high within the planted theory niche but evidence for real-transformer head specialization is low.
